research-methods-s1.title: Does a new caffeine-free energy drink improve reaction time?
research-methods-s1.html:
Introduction

A company claims its caffeine-free energy drink makes people react faster. Researchers tested the claim.

Participants

Eighty college students volunteered (ages 18 to 22, 44 women and 36 men) at one university.

Method

A computer randomly assigned each student to one of two groups. The experimental group drank the energy drink; the control group drank a look-alike drink with the same taste and color but none of the active ingredients. Neither the students nor the research assistants who ran the test knew which drink each student had. Twenty minutes later, each student pressed a key as fast as possible when a light flashed, 20 times. Reaction time was the average number of milliseconds between the flash and the key press.

Results

The experimental group’s average reaction time was 312 milliseconds; the control group’s was 318 milliseconds.

Discussion

The researchers concluded that the drink made at most a very small difference in reaction time.

Invented study for practice.

research-methods-s3.title: A school survey on homework and sleep
research-methods-s3.html:
Introduction

A student council wanted to know whether homework load is related to how much students sleep.

Participants

All 240 students in grades 9 to 12 at one high school were invited; 150 returned the form.

Method

Students answered two questions on a paper form with no name on it: "About how many hours of homework do you do on a school night?" and "About how many hours do you sleep on a school night?" They also rated the statement "I get enough sleep" from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree).

Results

Students who reported more homework also reported less sleep. The average rating of "I get enough sleep" was 2.1.

Invented study for practice.

research-sampling-s1.title: Does a daily 15-minute walk lift mood?
research-sampling-s1.html:
Introduction

Researchers tested whether a 15-minute walk outdoors each day improves mood over two weeks.

Participants

Researchers placed an ad in one city’s newspaper. Of 300 adults who answered, 120 were chosen at random to take part (ages 30 to 65; 70% women; most were retired or worked part time).

Method

A computer randomly assigned half the participants to take a 15-minute walk outdoors each day; the other half spent 15 minutes each day reading indoors. Before and after the two weeks, each person rated their mood from 1 (very low) to 7 (very high).

Results

Mood ratings rose by an average of 0.9 points in the walking group and by 0.2 points in the reading group.

Invented study for practice.

research-ethics-s1.title: Does a stressful speech task affect memory?
research-ethics-s1.html:
Introduction

Researchers asked whether preparing for a surprise speech affects how many words people remember.

Participants

Sixty university students (ages 18 to 24) took part. The university’s institutional review board approved the study. Each student read and signed a consent form that described a "memory task" and said they could stop at any time.

Method

Students were randomly assigned to two groups. One group was told they would soon give a speech that would be video-recorded and judged; the other group was not. In fact, no one gave a speech. All students then studied 20 words and wrote down as many as they could recall in two minutes.

Results

The speech group recalled an average of 9 words; the comparison group recalled 12.

Discussion

At the end of the session, researchers told each student that no speech had been planned, explained why the study needed this cover story, and answered their questions.

Invented study for practice.

Most participants recalled close to 12 words

items.q: What is the mean reaction time across all 10 trials, in milliseconds?

mistakes.why: That averages the four times in the table (280, 300, 320, 900) without counting how many trials had each. Multiply each time by its number of trials first.
3620 is the total of all 10 trials. Divide by 10.

items.q: What is the median reaction time, in milliseconds?

mistakes.why: 362 is the mean. The median is the middle of the ordered list.
That is halfway between 300 and 320, the middle of the table’s rows. Count trials: the 5th and 6th trials in order are both 300.

items.q: Which statistic gives the better summary of this participant’s usual reaction time, and why?
options: The median, because the 900 ms sneeze trial pulls the mean up
The mean, because it uses each trial, including the 900 ms one
The range, because it shows the fastest and slowest trials
The mode and the mean are equal, so either works

items.q: What is the range of the reaction times, in milliseconds?

mistakes.why: 40 is the range without the outlier (320 - 280). The range uses the highest value, 900.
900 is the highest value. Subtract the lowest, 280.

items.q: If the researcher drops the 900 ms trial as a recording error, what happens to the mean and the median?
options: Both drop by about the same amount
The mean drops a lot; the median stays at 300
The median drops a lot; the mean stays about the same
Neither changes, since one trial is a small part of the data

items.q: Which score range holds the most students?
Scores on a memory test are normally distributed with a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10. What is the z score of a student who scored 70?

mistakes.why: 20 is how many points above the mean the score is. Divide by the standard deviation, 10.
The score is above the mean, so z is positive.

items.q: On a test with a mean of 80 and a standard deviation of 5, what is the z score of a score of 75?

mistakes.why: The score is below the mean, so z is negative.
-5 is the distance in points. Divide by the standard deviation, 5.

items.q: By the 68-95-99.7 rule, what percent of scores in a normal distribution fall within two standard deviations of the mean?

mistakes.why: 47.5% is one side only. Add both sides of the mean.
68% is within one standard deviation. Two standard deviations hold 95%.

items.q: In a normal distribution, what percent of scores fall more than one standard deviation above the mean?

mistakes.why: 34% lies between the mean and one SD above it. Above one SD is what is left of the upper half: 50 - 34.
32% lies outside one SD on both sides together. Above it is half of that.

items.q: A student’s score is one standard deviation above the mean of a normal distribution. By the 68-95-99.7 rule, what is the student’s percentile rank?

mistakes.why: 34% is only the band between the mean and one SD. Add the 50% below the mean.
68% lies within one SD on both sides; it is not the percent below a score.

items.q: Maya scored at the 90th percentile on a reading test. What does that mean?
options: She scored higher than about 90% of test takers
She answered about 90% of the test questions correctly
Her score is 90 points above the mean
She is in the top 90% of the test takers

items.q: Ana scored 72 on a biology test (mean 60, standard deviation 6) and 85 on a history test (mean 80, standard deviation 10). On which test did she do better compared with the other students?

Biology, where her z score is +2
History, where her z score is +5
Equally well, since she was above the mean both times

items.q: By the 68-95-99.7 rule, what percent of test takers scored between 85 and 115?

mistakes.why: 34% is one side only, 100 to 115. Add 85 to 100.
95% is within two standard deviations, 70 to 130.

items.q: What percent of test takers scored above 130?

mistakes.why: 5% is outside two SDs on both sides together. Above 130 is only the upper half of that.
13.5% is the band from 115 to 130, below 130 rather than above it.

items.q: A student scored 70. What is that score’s z score?

mistakes.why: 70 is below the mean of 100, so z is negative.
-30 is the distance in points. Divide by the SD, 15.

items.q: Build an answer to: explain what the difference between the group means shows.

specific.frame: The ___ group reported ___ worry than the other group, and because the difference was statistically significant, ___.
specific.model: The walking group reported less worry (4.8) than the sitting group (5.6), and because the difference was statistically significant, it is unlikely to be due to chance alone.

statistic.label: Group and direction
options: walking group reported less
sitting group reported less
walking group reported more

why.1: The sitting group’s mean, 5.6, is higher: more worry.
why.2: The walking group’s mean, 4.8, is lower: less worry.

meaning.label: What significance means

it is unlikely to be due to chance alone
every student who walks will worry less

why.0: Significance is not size; the effect size was small.
why.2: Means describe groups, not every individual.
